svg.aria-label: Map from India to Japan showing the overland and maritime Buddhist routes into China and Wuyue's sea links to Korea and Japan

g.data-info: Great monastic university of Bihar. Xuanzang studied here in the 630s and carried hundreds of texts back to Chang’an.
Gateway from the Indian plains to the Silk Road passes; early home of Buddhist art and translators.
Oasis where caravans descended from the Pamirs into the Tarim Basin.
Home city of Kumārajīva (344–413), whose Chinese translations of the Lotus Sutra became the standard text.
Cave-temple complex at the China end of the desert route. Its sealed library preserved the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book.
Tang capital and the great translation centre. The Huichang persecution of 845 destroyed temples and libraries here and across China.
Bengal port where pilgrims such as Faxian and Yijing took ship for the east.
Capital of Sri Lanka; Faxian stayed two years copying texts before sailing home (c. 411).
Sumatran kingdom and Buddhist centre. Yijing spent years here studying Sanskrit (late 7th c.).
Main southern landfall for ships arriving from the Indian Ocean.
Capital of Wuyue. Home to Lingyin and Jingci temples, and to the Leifeng Pagoda (975), which held Qian Chu’s printed dhāraṇī sutra.
Modern Ningbo. Wuyue’s great port and the departure point for ships to Goryeo and Japan.
Goryeo capital. King Gwangjong sent monks to study with Yongming Yanshou in Hangzhou; in 961 the monk Chegwan sailed to Wuyue with Tiantai texts.
Buddhism officially received from the north in 372.
Kingdom that sent Buddhist images and sutras to the Japanese court in the 6th century (538 or 552).
Japan’s gateway office for foreign ships and envoys in Kyushu.
Japanese capital. Tendai texts and Wuyue’s miniature stupas reached temples in this region.
